title: Out of the depths (Psalm 130)
hookLine: a cry from the deep, said in the days before Yom Kippur
carry: more than watchmen for the morning

cards: Three in the morning, awake, staring at the ceiling. Something has gone badly wrong, or you've done something you regret, and it feels like you're at the bottom of a well, too far down for anyone to hear.
Everything polite has fallen away. What comes out, if anything comes out, isn't a speech. It's a cry.
There's a psalm for exactly that place, and it's only eight verses long.

teach.b: Psalm one thirty is one of fifteen psalms with the heading Song of Ascents.

The Mishnah describes fifteen steps in the Temple where the Levites stood and sang, and many connect these songs to those steps, or to pilgrims climbing up to Jerusalem. This one climbs from the very bottom.
"Out of the depths" have I called You, O Lord.

In Hebrew, mi-ma'amakim: the depths of the sea, the pit, the lowest place. Hasidic teachers love a second reading: not only from my deep trouble, but from deep inside me, the bottom of the heart, where nothing is fake.
If You kept a record of every wrong, Lord, who could stand? But with You there is forgiveness. The psalm doesn't pretend to be innocent.

Then its most beautiful image: my soul waits for the Lord more than watchmen wait for the morning. Picture a guard on the night shift, staring east for the first gray light that tells him the night is over.
The psalm says the line twice, as if the night is that long.
That's why, in many communities, this psalm is said every morning in the ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur: days for honest accounting, said from the depths, waiting for the light.

how: In many communities, Psalm 130 is said aloud in the morning service during the Ten Days of Repentance between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, and many people recite it in times of trouble.

o: a call to rise early for morning prayer
a plea for rain in a season of drought
from the depths, a cry from deep down

games.q: what's inside the psalm — tap the pairs.

s: Psalm 130 claims the one praying has done nothing wrong
it says: if You kept a record of every wrong, who could stand?
many communities say it during the ten days before Yom Kippur
days of honest accounting, said from the depths.
the psalm repeats its line about watchmen waiting for morning
said twice, as if the night is that long.

games.q: you're at the bottom of a well at three in the morning. you want to pray, but you have no fine words. what does Psalm 130 do?
o: wait until you feel better, then pray.
cry out from the depths, honestly.
games.why: it calls out from the depths, admits its wrongs, and waits more than watchmen wait for the morning.

practice: Go down, gently, to the lowest place in you right now: something you're sorry for, something you're afraid of, something you need.

Don't dress it up; find the fewest words that say it, maybe just help, or I'm sorry, or I'm scared, and say it inside, once, from the bottom. Then wait, the way a watchman waits for the morning, and if you pray, say it to God.

wordCard.voice: Mi-ma'amakim. From the depths, or from deep inside — Psalm one thirty's cry said in the days before Yom Kippur: my soul waits, more than watchmen for the morning.

orig.note: Hebrew: from the depths. The first word after the heading of Psalm 130.

carryVoice: Your line: more than watchmen for the morning. A cry from the depths, and then the waiting. Day three hundred twenty-four, done.
